title: Tags, Versions, and Releases
intro: Most release pipelines trigger on a version tag. Tags mark exactly which commit became v2.4.0 — so you can rebuild it, roll back to it, or audit it months later.

steps.why: SemVer carries meaning: bump PATCH for fixes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, MAJOR for breaking changes. Consumers and automation (dependency bots, changelogs) rely on it.

steps.prompt: Create an annotated tag v2.4.0 with a release message.
steps.explanation: Annotated tags store who tagged, when, and a message — lightweight tags (git tag v2.4.0) are just a pointer.
steps.why: Use annotated tags for releases: they carry metadata, can be signed, and are what 'git describe' uses by default.

steps.prompt: Push the tag to trigger the release pipeline.
steps.explanation: Tags aren't pushed by a normal 'git push' — they must be pushed explicitly.
steps.why: Release workflows commonly trigger on 'on: push: tags: ["v*"]'. Forgetting to push the tag is the usual reason 'the release pipeline never ran'.

steps.prompt: Show how the current commit relates to the most recent tag — useful for generating build version strings.
steps.why: Pipelines often stamp builds with this string so every artifact is traceable to an exact commit, even between releases.

steps.prompt: You tagged the wrong commit as v2.4.1 and already pushed it. Delete the tag locally and on the remote.
expected_commands: git tag -d v2.4.1 && git push origin --delete v2.4.1
git tag -d v2.4.1 && git push --delete origin v2.4.1
steps.explanation: Both the local and remote copies are removed.
steps.why: Do this only if nothing has consumed the tag yet. If a v2.4.1 artifact was already published, re-using that version for different code is worse than the mistake itself — release v2.4.2 instead. Published versions should be immutable.

steps.prompt: Create a GitHub release from the v2.4.0 tag with auto-generated release notes.
steps.explanation: Release notes are generated from merged PRs since the previous release.
steps.why: Consistent PR titles (the conventional-commit style from cicd-tutorial-001) are what make generated notes readable rather than a list of 'fix stuff'.
